questions.question: Which of the following is NOT the aim to establish the Directive Principles of State Policy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Political democracy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution and aim to create a framework for establishing a welfare state by guiding the government in policy-making and legislation. These principles are not enforceable by law but are fundamental in governance.
 
• The primary objectives of the DPSP include achieving **social justice**, ensuring **economic democracy**, and fostering **social democracy**. These are necessary for reducing inequalities in wealth, income, and opportunities.
 
• **Political democracy**, while an essential aspect of a democratic state, is not specifically addressed as an aim of the Directive Principles. Political democracy primarily concerns free and fair elections, individual rights, and political freedoms, which are guaranteed by other parts of the Constitution, notably the Fundamental Rights in Part III.
 
• The DPSP focuses on promoting an equitable society through measures like equal pay for equal work, protection of workers, promotion of education, public health, and living standards, and reducing the concentration of wealth (Articles 38–51).
 
• Thus, the goal of **political democracy** is distinct from the aims of the Directive Principles, which are more oriented towards creating a welfare state and ensuring economic and social justice. *Hence, the correct answer is Political democracy.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy:**

 
 
• The DPSP are inspired by the **Irish Constitution**, which in turn drew from the directive principles of social policy in the Spanish Constitution.
 
• These principles aim at ensuring socio-economic justice and serve as a guide for the state to establish policies that reduce disparities and ensure overall development.
 
• Examples include provisions for free and compulsory education for children (Article 45) and the promotion of the welfare of people through economic justice (Article 38).
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights and Political Democracy:**
 
 
• Political democracy is primarily upheld through **Fundamental Rights** (Part III) like the right to equality (Article 14–18), the right to freedom (Article 19–22), and the right to constitutional remedies (Article 32).
 
• These rights ensure that citizens can freely participate in the political process, express opinions, and seek protection against state excesses.
 
• Political democracy also involves periodic free and fair elections, which are conducted under the supervision of the **Election Commission of India**.
 
 
 
• **Key Articles of DPSP:**
 
 
• **Article 38:** Directs the state to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order marked by justice – social, economic, and political.
 
• **Article 39:** Calls for ensuring that the ownership and control of resources are distributed to serve the common good.
 
• **Article 41:** Directs the state to make effective provisions for securing the right to work, education, and public assistance.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of DPSP and Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights** are justiciable, meaning they are enforceable by courts, whereas **DPSP** are non-justiciable but act as guiding principles for governance.
 
• Fundamental Rights focus more on individual freedoms, while DPSP aims to achieve collective welfare.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Implementation of DPSP:**

 
 
• Many laws and policies in India, such as the **National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA)**, the **Mid-Day Meal Scheme**, and the **Right to Education Act**, derive inspiration from the DPSP.
 
• The **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments** for local self-governance also reflect the spirit of the DPSP.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Implementing DPSP:**
 
 
• Lack of adequate resources and political will often hampers the realization of these principles.
 
• Balancing DPSP with Fundamental Rights can sometimes lead to conflicts, as seen in cases like the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)**.

questions.question: As of July 2025, women in India represent only ______ of the STEM workforce, limiting women's access to career opportunities offered by the STEM sector.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.27**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• As of **July 2025**, women in **India** represent **27%** (or **0.27**) of the **STEM workforce**. This indicates a significant gender disparity in the STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) sector.
 
• The underrepresentation of women in STEM fields limits their **access to career opportunities** in these high-growth and lucrative areas.
 
• Globally, the percentage of women in STEM varies widely, but India’s **27% participation rate** highlights the need for focused measures to promote gender equity in these fields.
 
• One of the contributing factors is the lack of **inclusive policies** and **support systems** for women, including workplace flexibility, mentoring, and initiatives to reduce gender bias.
 
• The government and organizations are working towards increasing women's participation in STEM through **scholarships**, **awareness campaigns**, and **educational programs** to encourage girls to pursue careers in science and technology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Global Comparison:**

 
 
• Globally, women make up around **28-30%** of the STEM workforce on average, according to various reports such as UNESCO’s **Cracking the Code: Girls’ and Women’s Education in STEM**.
 
• Countries like the **United States** report a slightly higher percentage of women in STEM fields (around 35%), while the numbers are lower in **developing economies**.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Women in STEM:**
 
 
• **Socio-cultural norms:** Gender stereotypes and societal expectations often discourage women from pursuing STEM careers.
 
• **Lack of role models:** The absence of visible female leaders in STEM fields reduces inspiration for young girls to enter these areas.
 
• **Workplace challenges:** Gender biases, unequal pay, and limited opportunities for growth create barriers for women in STEM professions.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives in India:**
 
 
• The Government of India has launched several programs like the **Vigyan Jyoti Program** by the Department of Science & Technology (DST) to increase women's participation in STEM.
 
• Under the **New Education Policy (NEP) 2020**, emphasis is laid on promoting gender equality in education, including STEM disciplines.
 
• Efforts such as **scholarships for girls** in STEM fields and campaigns like **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** aim to bridge the gender gap.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of Women in STEM:**
 
 
• Studies show that increasing women’s participation in STEM can drive **innovation**, improve **economic outcomes**, and create more inclusive work environments.
 
• Diversity in STEM teams leads to **better problem-solving** and enhanced creativity, which benefits organizations and industries.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Statistics:**

 
 
• A report by **UNESCO** highlights that globally, **only 30%** of female students choose STEM-related fields in higher education.
 
• Fields like **engineering** and **computer science** have particularly low representation of women (**10-15%** in some countries).
 
 
 
• **Examples of STEM Role Models:**
 
 
• Prominent women in STEM include **Kalpana Chawla** (Astronaut), **Maryam Mirzakhani** (Mathematician), and **Dr. Tessy Thomas** (Indian Missile Scientist).
 
• Such role models inspire young girls to pursue careers in science and technology.

questions.question: As of June 2025, which of the following city has surpassed Mumbai to become the India's leopard capital?

__
 
• **बेंगलुरु** has surpassed **Mumbai** to become India's leopard capital as of **June 2025**.

• This change in leopard population density is attributed to better conservation efforts, improved wildlife corridors, and stricter anti-poaching measures in Karnataka.
 
• Leopards are highly adaptive animals, often thriving in urban fringes where they find abundant food and shelter.
 
• Studies and surveys by wildlife organizations such as the **Wildlife Institute of India** and the Karnataka Forest Department have confirmed this significant shift in leopard demographics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Leopards in India:**

 
 
• The leopard (**Panthera pardus fusca**) is one of the five big cats found in India, alongside the tiger, lion, snow leopard, and clouded leopard.
 
• Leopards are listed as **Vulnerable** on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (**IUCN**) Red List.
 
• They are widely distributed across India, from the Himalayas to the southernmost parts of the country.
 
 
 
• **Bannerghatta National Park:**
 
 
• Located near Bengaluru, this park is a significant habitat for leopards and other wildlife species.
 
• It acts as a critical wildlife corridor connecting various forest areas in Karnataka.
 
• Efforts to mitigate human-wildlife conflict in this region have contributed to the thriving leopard population.
 
 
 
• **Conservation Challenges:**
 
 
• Leopards often come into conflict with humans due to habitat encroachment and urbanization.
 
• Poaching and illegal wildlife trade remain significant threats to their survival.
 
• State governments and wildlife organizations are working on creating awareness and implementing conservation measures.
 
 
 
• **Leopard Census in India:**
 
 
• The **All India Leopard Census 2018** estimated the leopard population in India to be around **12,852**.
 
• The census highlighted a positive growth in leopard numbers in states like **Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Uttarakhand** due to focused conservation efforts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Human-Wildlife Coexistence:**

 
 
• In regions like Bengaluru, initiatives to manage leopard-human interactions have been crucial in minimizing conflicts.
 
• Measures include setting up **camera traps**, creating awareness among local communities, and establishing rapid response teams.
 
 
 
• **State’s Role in Wildlife Conservation:**
 
 
• The Karnataka Forest Department has been proactive in implementing wildlife conservation policies.
 
• Programs such as the **Project Leopard** aim to ensure the long-term survival of leopards in the state.

questions.question: The Darbhanga gayaki of Dhrupad, a classical form of Indian music, is associated with which Indian state/UT?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bihar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Darbhanga Gharana** is one of the prominent styles of **Dhrupad singing**, a classical form of Indian music.
 
• Dhrupad is considered one of the oldest genres of Hindustani classical music, dating back to the **16th century**.
 
• The Darbhanga style is named after **Darbhanga**, a city in the state of Bihar, where this tradition flourished under royal patronage.
 
• The style is known for its emphasis on **rhythmic variations** and intricate compositions, performed in a slow and meditative manner.
 
• Prominent musicians from the Darbhanga Gharana include **Padma Shri Ram Chatur Mallik** and **Prem Kumar Mallik**, who have contributed significantly to preserving this tradition.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Significance of Dhrupad:**

 
 
• Dhrupad originated in the temples of India as devotional music dedicated to deities like **Lord Shiva**.
 
• It was later adapted for court performances during the reign of **Akbar**, who was a patron of Dhrupad and employed musicians like **Tansen**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of Dhrupad:**
 
 
• Dhrupad compositions typically consist of a slow and deliberate alaap (introduction), followed by rhythmic sections called **jor** and **jhala**.
 
• It is performed in Sanskrit or Braj Bhasha and emphasizes purity of raga and tonal quality.
 
 
 
• **Other Dhrupad Gharanas:**
 
 
• In addition to the Darbhanga Gharana, notable styles include the **Bettiah Gharana** (also from Bihar), the **Dagur Gharana**, and the **Khandar Gharana**.
 
• Each gharana has distinct features in terms of vocal presentation and composition structure.
 
 
 
• **Present-Day Scenario:**
 
 
• Efforts are being made to revive Dhrupad through institutions like the **Dhrupad Sansthan** in Madhya Pradesh and the **ITC Sangeet Research Academy** in Kolkata.
 
• Contemporary musicians continue to perform Dhrupad on global platforms, showcasing the rich heritage of Indian classical music.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bihar’s Contribution to Music:**

 
 
• Bihar has been home to several classical music traditions, including Dhrupad and folk music like **Bhojpuri** songs.
 
• Darbhanga and Bettiah have historically been centers of musical excellence in the state.
 
 
 
• **Preservation of Dhrupad:**
 
 
• Institutions and government bodies are working toward documenting and promoting Dhrupad to prevent its decline.
 
• Scholarships and grants are provided to aspiring musicians to learn and practice this art form.

__
 
• **Swami and Friends** is the first novel in the trilogy written by **R.K. Narayan**. It was published in **1935**, marking his debut as a novelist.
 
• The trilogy, also known as the Malgudi series, includes three novels: **Swami and Friends**, **The Bachelor of Arts**, and **The English Teacher**.
 
• The novel is set in the fictional town of **Malgudi**, which R.K. Narayan created as the backdrop for many of his literary works.

questions.question: Which of the following relates to those expenses incurred for the normal functioning of the government departments?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Revenue expenditure**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Revenue expenditure** refers to the expenses incurred for the day-to-day functioning of government departments and services. These are recurring expenses and do not create assets.
 
• It includes spending on salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest payments on loans, and other administrative costs required for running government operations.
 
• Such expenditures are essential for maintaining the normal functioning of the government and ensuring the provision of public services like healthcare, education, and infrastructure maintenance.
 
• Revenue expenditure is financed through revenue receipts, such as tax revenues (direct and indirect taxes) and non-tax revenues (fees, fines, and dividends from public sector enterprises).
 
• Unlike capital expenditure, revenue expenditure does not result in the creation of long-term assets and is entirely consumed during the fiscal year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Capital expenditure:**

 
 
• Capital expenditure is used for acquiring or maintaining fixed assets, such as buildings, land, machinery, and infrastructure.
 
• It contributes to the creation of long-term assets that aid in economic growth and development.
 
• Examples include construction of highways, railways, airports, and purchase of equipment for public services.
 
• Unlike revenue expenditure, this type of spending has a lasting impact and enhances the productive capacity of the economy.
 
 
 
• **Revenue receipt:**
 
 
• Revenue receipts include all the income generated by the government through taxes and non-tax sources.
 
• Examples of tax revenue include income tax, corporate tax, GST, and customs duties.
 
• Non-tax revenue sources include fees, fines, dividends from public enterprises, and grants from foreign governments.
 
• Revenue receipts are used to finance revenue expenditure and do not create liabilities or reduce assets.
 
 
 
• **Capital receipt:**
 
 
• Capital receipts are funds raised by the government through loans, disinvestment, and recovery of loans.
 
• These receipts either create liabilities (such as borrowing) or result in a reduction of assets (such as selling public assets).
 
• Examples include issuing bonds, external loans, and proceeds from the sale of government-owned enterprises.
 
• Capital receipts are used to finance both capital and revenue expenditure.
 
 
 
• **Key distinction:**
 
 
• **Revenue expenditure:** Does not create assets and is recurring in nature.
 
• **Capital expenditure:** Creates assets and has long-term implications for economic growth.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Budget Classification:**

 
 
• The government budget is divided into revenue budget (covering revenue receipts and revenue expenditure) and capital budget (covering capital receipts and capital expenditure).
 
• Both components are essential for ensuring economic stability and proper management of public finances.
 
 
 
• **Examples of Revenue Expenditure:**
 
 
• Payment of salaries and pensions to government employees.
 
• Subsidies on food, fertilizers, and petroleum products.
 
• Interest payments on government borrowings.
 
• Expenses on public administration, defense, and social welfare schemes.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal Responsibility:**
 
 
• The government aims to control revenue expenditure to avoid fiscal deficits and ensure efficient use of public funds.
 
• Excessive revenue expenditure can lead to inflation and debt accumulation, which may harm economic stability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The FIPB was responsible for **processing FDI proposals** requiring government approval and ensuring compliance with India's FDI policy.

• It aimed to ensure that foreign investments aligned with India's development goals and national interests.
 
 
 
• **Abolition of the FIPB:**

• The PMO plays a vital role in coordinating between various ministries and departments to ensure smooth governance and implementation of policies.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Economic Reforms in 1991:**

• The establishment of the FIPB was a key measure under these reforms to attract foreign investment and modernize India's economy.

• **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI):**

• **FDI in India:** India has emerged as a significant destination for FDI due to its large consumer market, skilled workforce, and favorable government policies.

Which type of bill cannot originate in the State Legislative Council of an Indian state?

I. Money Bill

II. Ordinary Bill
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only I**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Money Bills** cannot originate in the **State Legislative Council**. They can only originate in the **State Legislative Assembly**, as per **Article 198** of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• A **Money Bill** deals with taxation, public expenditure, borrowing of money by the government, or matters related to the Consolidated Fund of the state.
 
• The **State Legislative Assembly** has the exclusive power to discuss and pass a Money Bill. The Legislative Council, where it exists, can only provide recommendations, which the Assembly may accept or reject.
 
• Ordinary Bills, on the other hand, can originate in either the **State Legislative Assembly** or the **State Legislative Council**, where a bicameral system exists.
 
• Therefore, the statement "Money Bill cannot originate in the State Legislative Council" is **correct**, while the statement for Ordinary Bills is **incorrect**. Hence, **Only I is correct.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Money Bill:**

 
 
• A Money Bill is defined under **Article 110** of the Indian Constitution at the Union level and **Article 198** at the state level.
 
• It exclusively deals with financial matters like taxation, public expenditure, and government borrowings.
 
• The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly has the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill.
 
• The role of the State Legislative Council, if present, is advisory; they must return the bill to the Assembly within **14 days**, with or without recommendations.
 
• The Assembly is not bound to accept the recommendations made by the Legislative Council.
 
 
 
• **Ordinary Bill:**
 
 
• Unlike a Money Bill, an Ordinary Bill can originate in either the Legislative Assembly or the Legislative Council in states with a bicameral legislature.
 
• Both Houses must pass the Ordinary Bill before it is sent to the Governor for assent.
 
• If there is a disagreement between the two Houses, the decision of the Legislative Assembly prevails.
 
 
 
• **Bicameral System in India:**
 
 
• Only a few Indian states have a bicameral legislature, including **Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana**.
 
• In these states, the legislature comprises two Houses: the **Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha)** and the **Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad)**.
 
• In states with a unicameral system, there is only a Legislative Assembly, and all bills originate and are passed within this single House.
 
 
 
• **Important Articles of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• **Article 198:** Deals with Money Bills in state legislatures.
 
• **Article 199:** Defines the scope of what constitutes a Money Bill.
 
• **Article 200:** Outlines the Governor's role in assenting to bills passed by the state legislature.
 
• **Article 110:** Defines Money Bills at the Union level.
 
• **Article 111:** Discusses the President's role in assenting to Money Bills.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The State Legislative Council’s powers are limited when compared to the Legislative Assembly, especially for Money Bills.
 
• The existence of a Legislative Council in a state is optional. A state can abolish or create a Legislative Council through a resolution passed by the Legislative Assembly and approved by Parliament.
 
• The decision-making authority for financial matters in a state rests primarily with the Legislative Assembly.
 
• The bicameral system is aimed at providing a system of checks and balances but is limited in its scope for financial legislation.
 
• The Governor's assent is mandatory for all bills (Money or Ordinary) passed by the state legislature before they become laws.

questions.question: The Konkan Railway connects ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Roha and Mangalore**__.

__
 
• The **Konkan Railway** is a major railway line in India that connects **Roha** in Maharashtra to **Mangalore** in Karnataka.
 
• The railway line runs parallel to the **Konkan Coast**, covering regions in Maharashtra, Goa, and Karnataka.
 
• It spans a total distance of approximately **741 kilometers**, making it one of the longest railway routes in India.
 
• Known for its engineering marvels, the Konkan Railway features **numerous tunnels, bridges, and viaducts** across the picturesque Western Ghats.
 
• The railway is highly significant for providing connectivity to remote areas along the Konkan coastline, facilitating trade, tourism, and travel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background:**

 
 
• The **Konkan Railway Corporation Limited (KRCL)** was established in **1990** to oversee the construction and operation of the railway line.
 
• The first passenger train service on the Konkan Railway was inaugurated on **26 January 1998**.
 
 
 
• **Engineering Features:**
 
 
• The railway passes through **91 tunnels**, the longest being the **Karbude Tunnel**, which is 6.5 kilometers long.
 
• It has over **2,000 bridges**, including the **Panval Nadi Viaduct**, which is one of the tallest viaducts in India.
 
 
 
• **Geographical Importance:**
 
 
• The line runs through the rugged terrain of the **Western Ghats**, offering scenic views of valleys, waterfalls, and forests.
 
• It connects the coastal regions of Maharashtra, Goa, and Karnataka, which are vital for **tourism and trade**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• The railway has boosted the economy of the Konkan region by providing faster and more efficient transportation options.
 
• It facilitates the movement of goods such as agricultural products, seafood, and industrial goods.
 
 
 
• **Tourism Benefits:**
 
 
• Popular destinations along the route include **Goa**, **Ratnagiri**, and **Karwar**, attracting tourists from across India.
 
• Special trains such as the **Madgaon-Mumbai Konkan Kanya Express** provide scenic travel experiences.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Konkan Railway is renowned for being an **engineering marvel**, overcoming challenges posed by the Western Ghats' rugged terrain.
 
• It has significantly reduced travel time between **Mumbai** and **Mangalore**, benefiting both passengers and freight transport.
 
• The railway uses advanced technologies such as **anti-collision devices (ACD)** to enhance safety.
 
• It operates in a region prone to heavy rainfall, requiring the use of **innovative drainage systems** to prevent flooding and landslides.

questions.question: In India, the second five year plan ended in which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1961**__.

__
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan** in India was implemented from **1956 to 1961**, ending in the year **1961**.
 
• This plan was based on the **P.C. Mahalanobis model**, emphasizing the growth of the industrial sector and heavy industries in India.
 
• The focus was on **rapid industrialization**, particularly in sectors like iron, steel, heavy machinery, and infrastructure development.
 
• The plan aimed to reduce reliance on agriculture and shift towards a more industrialized economy to achieve long-term economic growth.
 
• It also emphasized the importance of public sector enterprises and aimed to promote a **socialistic pattern of society**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **First Five-Year Plan (1951–1956):**

 
 
• Focused on **agriculture, irrigation, and energy**.
 
• Aimed at addressing food shortages and rehabilitating the economy after independence.
 
• Key projects: **Bhakra Nangal Dam** and **Hirakud Dam**.
 
 
 
• **Second Five-Year Plan (1956–1961):**
 
 
• Emphasized the development of **heavy industries** and **public sector enterprises**.
 
• Introduced the **P.C. Mahalanobis model**, focusing on capital goods production.
 
• Major industries developed: **steel plants in Bhilai, Durgapur, and Rourkela**.
 
 
 
• **Third Five-Year Plan (1961–1966):**
 
 
• Aimed at achieving self-reliance in food production and setting up a diversified industrial base.
 
• Faced challenges due to the **Indo-China war (1962)** and **Indo-Pak war (1965)**.
 
• Plan period experienced significant agricultural setbacks.
 
 
 
• **Mahalanobis Model:**
 
 
• Developed by **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis**, an eminent Indian statistician.
 
• Focused on the growth of the industrial sector to achieve long-term economic growth.
 
• Advocated investment in capital goods industries to accelerate economic development.
 
 
 
• **Public Sector Enterprises:**
 
 
• Key component of the Second Five-Year Plan.
 
• Initiated several large-scale projects to boost industrial output and economic self-reliance.
 
• Major projects: **Bokaro Steel Plant**, **Heavy Engineering Corporation**, and **Oil refineries**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan** laid the foundation for India's industrialization, marking a shift from an agrarian economy to an industrial one.
 
• Introduced measures for the **promotion of small-scale industries** and entrepreneurship.
 
• Faced criticism for neglecting agriculture, leading to food shortages and increased imports.
 
• The plan's success was instrumental in shaping India's long-term economic strategies and vision.

questions.question: As per MOSPI report of 2024, sex ratio of India by 2036 will be ______.
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **sex ratio** refers to the number of females per 1,000 males in a population. It is a critical demographic indicator used to evaluate gender balance.
 
• According to the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI)** report for 2024, the projected sex ratio of India for the year **2036** is expected to be **952 females per 1,000 males**.
 
• This projection indicates a steady improvement in the sex ratio, reflecting efforts made by the government and society to address gender disparities.
 
• The increase in sex ratio can be attributed to initiatives such as **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao**, women empowerment programs, and improved awareness regarding gender equality.
 
• The sex ratio is calculated using census data and population surveys conducted by organizations like **MOSPI**, ensuring accuracy and reliability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sex Ratio Trends in India:**

 
 
• The sex ratio in India has historically been skewed in favor of males due to factors like **gender discrimination**, **female infanticide**, and **prenatal sex determination**.
 
• In the **2011 Census**, India's sex ratio stood at **940 females per 1,000 males**, showing gradual improvement over previous decades.
 
• Efforts to improve the sex ratio have included government schemes such as **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao**, which aim to eliminate gender biases and promote the welfare of girls.
 
 
 
• **MOSPI Role and Reports:**
 
 
• The **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI)** is responsible for compiling and analyzing data related to various socio-economic indicators.
 
• MOSPI’s projections are based on data collected through surveys like the **National Sample Survey (NSS)** and **Population Census**.
 
• The sex ratio projection for **2036** highlights the expected demographic changes over time due to policy interventions and changing societal norms.
 
 
 
• **Factors Affecting Sex Ratio:**
 
 
• Social practices such as **dowry** and **son preference** have historically contributed to a lower sex ratio.
 
• Improved education for women, better healthcare, and awareness campaigns are critical factors in enhancing the sex ratio.
 
• Legislative measures like the **Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994** have been implemented to prevent sex-selective abortion.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Countries:**
 
 
• India's sex ratio is lower than many developed countries, which often have ratios closer to **1,000 females per 1,000 males**.
 
• Countries like **Sweden** and **Norway** have nearly balanced sex ratios due to their strong emphasis on gender equality and social welfare systems.
 
• India’s progress in this area is significant but requires sustained effort to reach parity.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Data:**

 
 
• India's sex ratio in **1951** was **946 females per 1,000 males**, which declined over the decades before improving again in recent years.
 
• The **2001 Census** reported a sex ratio of **933 females per 1,000 males**, highlighting the need for intervention.
 
 
 
• **Government Schemes:**
 
 
• **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao:** Launched in **2015**, this scheme aims to address declining child sex ratios and promote gender equality.
 
• **Kishori Shakti Yojana:** Focuses on empowering adolescent girls through education and skill development.
 
• **National Rural Health Mission (NRHM):** Includes provisions for maternal and child healthcare to improve survival rates for female infants.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• Countries like **China** also face similar challenges due to historical policies like the **One-Child Policy**, which led to gender imbalances.
 
• International organizations like **UNICEF** and **WHO** advocate for gender equality as a global priority.
